issues.html:
Software Lead Weekly




Issue #727, 30th October 2026


ARCHIVE

This Week's Favorite

The Revised Rules of Engineering Management With Will Larson (Video)
116 minutes read.

This is the classic ZIRP hangover: when managers were told never to make technical decisions, the only levers left were headcount and process. Will Larson explains how that created bloated orgs, over-protected engineers, and surveys used as a verdict instead of a conversation starter. I like his reminder that in a world where code is cheap, the leader who can go back to the details has a real edge. Listen to it on your commute to work, it will be time well spent.

Read it later via Instapaper.
Share it via Twitter or email.

Culture

Whose Kid Is This
1 minutes read.

My humble effort to help you start the weekend with a smile.

Read it later via Instapaper.
Share it via Twitter or email.

Experts Lead Experts
3 minutes read.

I like the practical lesson hidden in this piece by Marty Cagan: the best technology managers got hands-on with AI to understand its nature, then went back to the bigger decisions. Use it to check your own leadership: do you know the tools well enough to judge your team's work and where the real constraint is now that building is cheap?

Read it later via Instapaper.
Share it via Twitter or email.

Writing Is No Longer Proof of Work
5 minutes read.

The biggest takeaway for dealing with meat proxy or AI slop is to demand concise writing. This forces the writer to distill their idea and land their main arguments effectively for readers. Ernest Hemingway wrote it well before: "All you have to do is write one true sentence. Write the truest sentence that you know."

Read it later via Instapaper.
Share it via Twitter or email.

Design as a Garden: A Different Way to Think About Creative Work.
3 minutes read.

"Match effort to the season. Ask yourself: does this need more effort, or simply more time? Practice patience. And when the time is ripe, work intensely." Justin Jay Wang shares a useful filter for leaders who default to adding more people or pressure when a project stalls.

Read it later via Instapaper.
Share it via Twitter or email.

Peopleware

Brand Is Who You Are
3 minutes read.

The logo and website are expressions of the brand, not the brand itself. You can hire someone to make a beautiful identity, but if it isn't connected to what the people behind the company believe, you are mostly choosing an appearance. With AI making polished output nearly free, that hollowness will be easier to spot.

Read it later via Instapaper.
Share it via Twitter or email.

Steve Jobs Took 19 Seconds to Name the Biggest Lesson Apple Taught Him: “When I See Something Not Being Done Right, My First Reaction Isn’t to Go Fix It.” (Video)
2 minutes read.

Steve Jobs shares the lesson Apple taught him: "When I see something not being done right, my first reaction isn't to go fix it." -- I like this as a check for any leader who got promoted for being the best fixer. Every time you jump in, the team learns that quality is your job. What is the last thing you fixed yourself that really signaled something about your system?

Read it later via Instapaper.
Share it via Twitter or email.

How to Pitch Really Damn Well
3 minutes read.

Worth reading even if you never plan to raise money. Aaron Harris argues that walking people through your operational complexity loses them, and that you should show how your current work leads to changing something foundational. Use it as a checklist on your next strategy doc: does it describe the world your team is building toward, or only the optimizations you did to get here?

Read it later via Instapaper.
Share it via Twitter or email.

Inspiring Tweets

@_oghenemaro: Devote the rest of your life in making progress.

@trq212: There’s 100% a kind of mania you can get into with coding agents, where it feels like you’re getting a lot done and working all the time but nothing is really happening. I think it's often a form of avoidance of something else in life.

- Oren

issues.title: Issue #726
issues.html:
Software Lead Weekly




Issue #726, 23rd October 2026


ARCHIVE

This Week's Favorite

How to Scale Intent, Quality, and Artistry With Al (Video)
22 minutes read.

Great talk by Katie Dill (Stripe) on keeping craft alive in the AI building boom: "Previously, a quality filter was essentially built into every stage of the product development process [...] Now we can generate 20 ideas a week. [...] the filtering that used to be throughout the process now has to happen after creation, when it's much harder to say 'no.'" -- I agree, and it makes the editor the most underrated role in an AI-heavy org: someone who looks at the whole product end to end, not each shiny piece. Who plays that role on your team today?

Read it later via Instapaper.
Share it via Twitter or email.

Culture

LGTM (Looks Good to Me) - Claude Opus 5.5 Music Video
1 minutes read.

My humble effort to help you start the weekend with a smile.

Read it later via Instapaper.
Share it via Twitter or email.

Good Interfaces Make Good Neighbors
3 minutes read.

Andrew Bosworth's checklist (owner, ordered priorities, process for new work) is getting much easier to follow. With the right context and AI to wrap it nicely, we can draw these interfaces and keep them up to date with minimal manual effort, which was the real reason they used to rot.

Read it later via Instapaper.
Share it via Twitter or email.

If Your Team Is Too Busy Doing Their 'Normal Job' to Experiment With AI, You're Preparing Them to Be Replaced
4 minutes read.

Great provocation by Geoffrey Huntley for any engineering leader. His claim is that "too busy" is a leadership choice, not a fact about the team, and that the gap between engineers who use AI and those who don't will show up (probably already showing up) in performance rankings within months. AI fluency is a visible skill to own, not an optional hobby.

Read it later via Instapaper.
Share it via Twitter or email.

Assorted Things I've Been Mulling Over Regarding Agents in the Economy
3 minutes read.

Patrick Collison shares a useful framing on what personal agents change for companies: "Personal agents will, I think, act as a kind of structural subsidy for product quality. How would markets look different if individuals always spent at least 10 hours researching their purchases? On the margin, focusing on making a product better is, I think, going to become a more effective strategy for companies." The same applies to how we build products with AI: if the buyer is an agent, distribution tricks and attention hacks matter less, and the quality of the core experience (and the data that proves it) matters more.

Read it later via Instapaper.
Share it via Twitter or email.

Peopleware

I Am Often Wrong (Boris Cherny, the Creator of Claude Code)
3 minutes read.

This should be part of Boris's README on how he drives decisions (I created [https://managerreadme.com](http://managerreadme.com "‌") years ago to address it from a management perspective). With AI making it cheap to build almost anything, a fuzzy problem now produces complex plans and unclear success criteria faster than ever.

Read it later via Instapaper.
Share it via Twitter or email.

You Have More Influence Over the Future Than You Think
6 minutes read.

Great short read to forward to your team before the next roadmap or planning session. Sharif Shameem notes that daily life looks much like 50 years ago, and that people who see AI only as a way to automate knowledge work lack imagination. Read it for the closing line, "the best way to predict the future is to invent it", then ask what you would build if your goal were improving customers' lives, not just making work more efficient.

Read it later via Instapaper.
Share it via Twitter or email.

Room for Ambition
3 minutes read.

Karri Saarinen (founder of Linear) describes what a team culture can give people: "You don't need to agree with every idea. But there is a room, or an environment, that gives ambition space. Often, the support is simple: listening seriously, sharing an idea or a story, making an introduction. Helping where you can without assuming you know what someone should do." I like this as a definition of what leaders can offer their teams.

Read it later via Instapaper.
Share it via Twitter or email.

Inspiring Tweets

@readswithravi: “If you can overthink the worst why can't you overthink the best.”

@hadari_o: Sure, blame Claude for your change that trashed prod but take credit for the html report "you made"

- Oren

issues.title: Issue #725
issues.html:
Software Lead Weekly




Issue #725, 16th October 2026


ARCHIVE

This Week's Favorite

The UI Is Not the Product: When Agents Do the Work, What's the Shape of the Product That Remains?
6 minutes read.

Great take by John Moriarty on where design effort goes once agents do the work: the approval moment: "The surface we author will get thinner, but the end-user experience will be richer. One question might pull from multiple sources, collapsing what used to be three separate tasks into one answer. [...] As Agents absorb more of the interface, what’s left to design gets smaller and more consequential. Fewer screens, each carrying more weight. The way you get those right is by deeply understanding the system underneath, because that’s what now drives the experience."

Read it later via Instapaper.
Share it via Twitter or email.

Culture

Best Resume I've Seen So Far
1 minutes read.

My humble effort to help you start the weekend with a smile.

Read it later via Instapaper.
Share it via Twitter or email.

Predictability vs Outcomes
4 minutes read.

I love this framing by Marty Cagan: "The real trade-off is the relative priority of outcomes versus predictability." Read it again. Outputs make it easier to predict when something is ready, not its value. Don't confuse features with dates to impact if you didn't verify the value first. If you can't verify it beforehand, at least focus on learning as much as you can by observing how users interact with the new feature and talking with them about it.

Read it later via Instapaper.
Share it via Twitter or email.

Zapier's CEO Will Grade Your AI PM Skills Live (Video)
74 minutes read.

Great watch for anyone leading product teams. Wade Foster on the transformational level: "If a factory produces a defective part, what does the worker do? Does he try to fix each part individually? No, not really. He just rejects a batch, checks the equipment and asks himself: Why did the machine produce these defective parts? [...] And that's what the work is actually shifting to." -- This is the playbook for agentic engineering orgs too: the leader's job moves from reviewing every output to auditing the system that produced it, and deciding where the human checkpoints sit.

Read it later via Instapaper.
Share it via Twitter or email.

Building a Second-Wave AI Business
7 minutes read.

Most businesses want to grow more than they want to optimize what they have. It's harder to predict what will drive higher revenue growth than to automate well-defined areas, so we're tempted to focus there. Seth is a master at narrowing down incentives and strategy to help you seek growth opportunities (relevant to everyone, and maybe more so for a bootstrapper who's aiming to get "default to live" urgently). If you map out your investment, how much of your time is invested in growth? How much is in optimization? Do you think the ratios serve the business or serve predictability?

Read it later via Instapaper.
Share it via Twitter or email.

Peopleware

What It Takes to Run Inbound Sales With AI (Video)
13 minutes read.

This is the playbook for any agentic product: start with the prompt to learn, then pull the deterministic parts into code so you can debug which rule fired instead of reading what the model said. Jeanne Grosser (COO at Vercel) shares how they built a machine that yields 90% of Vercel's inbound leads for roughly $ 1,000 per year.

Read it later via Instapaper.
Share it via Twitter or email.

15 Leadership Interview Questions and Answers to Find Great Leaders.
8 minutes read.

"Don't judge decisions solely by their outcomes. Explore the reasoning behind them and whether the candidate would make the same choice again." -- Stephanie Bowker shares this in a list of leadership interview questions. I agree, and it matters even more with AI in the loop: when agents make the first draft of every decision, the reasoning and tradeoffs a leader can articulate become the scarce skill to hire for.

Read it later via Instapaper.
Share it via Twitter or email.

How to Effectively Debug When You No Longer Understand the Code
30 minutes read.

This is the most comprehensive view I've read on debugging with agents, from three real production bugs to a full framework and what it means for your software factory. Cindy Sridharan puts the shift well: "What ought to replace [the mental model of the code] isn't a better mental model of the code [...] but a better methodology for reliably and repeatably reasoning about outcomes. [...] The engineers who thrive in an agent-native world will be the ones who are good at designing such verification loops, whether or not they understand the code it verifies." -- I agree, and it's the same playbook for agentic products: the value moves from knowing the code to designing the checks that keep an agent honest.

Read it later via Instapaper.
Share it via Twitter or email.

Inspiring Tweets

@paulg: If customers won't buy your stuff, try asking what they would buy. This sounds obvious, but surprisingly few founders do it, and it often yields valuable insights.

@shreyas: Something that’s changed rapidly in the past year: Product Managers who’ve historically viewed their role as “my main job is to execute” are finding it way harder to get hired at top companies than those who’ve viewed their role as “my main job is to make the product successful”

- Oren
